cards.title: Parity games in polynomial time
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(A\) and integers \(C,c\geq1\) such that, for every encoded finite parity game \(G\) and starting vertex \(s\), \(A\) decides whether Even has a winning strategy from \(s\) within \(C(L+1)^c\) steps, where \(L\) is the full input length defined below?
cards.definitions:
A parity game has vertices \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\geq1\), an edge relation \(E\subseteq V\times V\), an owner function \(o:V\to\{\mathrm{Even},\mathrm{Odd}\}\), and priorities \(p:V\to\mathbb N\), where \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Each vertex has at least one outgoing edge; self-loops are allowed. The designated start is \(s\in V\). An infinite play is a sequence \((v_i)_{i\geq0}\) with \(v_0=s\) and \((v_i,v_{i+1})\in E\) for every \(i\). The owner of \(v_i\) chooses \(v_{i+1}\); ownership need not alternate along an edge. Both players see the entire finite history and there are no chance moves. Let \(I=\{d\in\mathbb N:p(v_i)=d\text{ for infinitely many }i\}\). This set is finite and nonempty. Even wins precisely when \(\min I\) is even, and Odd wins otherwise.

A strategy for a player assigns a legal successor to every finite valid history ending at a vertex owned by that player. A play is consistent with the strategy if it follows the prescribed successor at each such vertex. Even has a winning strategy from \(s\) if there exists a strategy for which every consistent infinite play starting at \(s\) is won by Even. Strategies and infinite plays are quantified mathematical objects; neither is supplied as input. A positional strategy depends only on the current vertex, but the target does not assume positionality in its definition.

For a nonnegative integer \(a\), let \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^b0\operatorname{bin}(a+1)\), where \(b\) is the length of the binary expansion without leading zeroes. Encode a game by \(1^n0\), followed by its \(n^2\) adjacency bits in row order, \(n\) owner bits (0 for Even and 1 for Odd), then \(\operatorname{code}(p(1)),\ldots,\operatorname{code}(p(n)),\operatorname{code}(s)\), with no trailing bits. The input length \(L\) includes every priority bit. Invalid encodings are rejected within the same polynomial time bound. The machine is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program, finite tape alphabet and no oracle or advice; each transition costs one step. All arithmetic and input processing count toward time. The same \(A,C,c\) must work for every arena and all priority values, with no fixed bound on the number or magnitude of priorities.

context_blocks.text: The original source asks about computing winning regions: all vertices from which each player can force a win. A polynomial-time decider for one specified vertex computes these regions by making one call per vertex, and a region algorithm answers the single-vertex question immediately. Thus the present decision target preserves the original polynomial-time question.

Every vertex is winning for exactly one player, and each player has a positional strategy winning from every vertex in its region. Consequently the winner problem lies in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\), and in fact in \(\mathrm{UP}\cap\mathrm{coUP}\). These inclusions do not supply a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm. The close connection to modal \(\mu\)-calculus model checking explains the problem’s role in verification.

The minimum-priority convention is equivalent to the maximum-priority convention used in some references: replace every priority \(p(v)\) by \(D-p(v)\), with an even integer \(D\geq\max_v p(v)\). This reverses order and preserves parity, using only polynomially many bit operations. Large numerical priorities can also be replaced, in sorted order, by increasing nonnegative priorities of the same respective parities, all at most \(2n-1\). This explains why binary priority values do not change the standard polynomial-time question.

Calude and coauthors established a deterministic quasipolynomial-time algorithm in 2017, meaning a bound of the form \(\exp((\log(L+2))^{O(1)})\). This was a major improvement, but such a bound need not be polynomial. Their paper also explicitly relates alternating-turn and vertex-owner conventions.

Czerwiński and coauthors prove quasipolynomial size lower bounds for the strong separating safety automata defined in their paper. This limits a broad collection of known constructions; it is not a lower bound against all deterministic parity-game algorithms.

Rick van der Heijden’s preprint of 4 November 2025 claims an algorithm taking \(O(n^2(n+m))\) time, with \(n\) vertices and \(m\) edges. Its Theorems 5, 7 and 8 assert correctness and the polynomial bound. The checked arXiv record still has only version 1. This review inspected the claim and theorem statements but did not establish their correctness or locate an authoritative primary-source resolution of the claim.

The 24 June 2026 revision of Suilen and Pérez’s paper, marked accepted at CONCUR 2026, continues to describe polynomial-time parity-game solving as open. Its Proposition 4.1 reduces parity games to a robust discounted-reward problem. That later treatment does not itself refute the 2025 algorithm claim; the current status remains explicitly unverified.

cards.why: Parity games are a central algorithmic component of model checking and reactive synthesis: they express recurring obligations in infinite executions by a finite arena. Their winner problem is polynomial-time equivalent to model checking the modal \(\mu\)-calculus. Determining whether general parity games admit polynomial time would resolve a basic complexity boundary for these verification tasks and for a natural problem in \(\mathrm{UP}\cap\mathrm{coUP}\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-verified proof of the stated existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a uniform algorithm and prove its termination, correctness for all valid games and polynomial bit-time bound, including rejection of malformed inputs. A negative answer must exclude every such polynomial-time decider for the full problem. A lower bound for a particular algorithm, automaton representation or restricted collection of methods does not prove that negation. Bounds whose polynomial exponent depends on the number of priorities, experimental performance, and conditional theorems do not settle the unconditional target.

importance.reason: A defining algorithmic question of verification and infinite-duration games, with direct modal-logic and synthesis connections and a major quasipolynomial breakthrough. Its former rank came from a provisional unassessed score, not a low-significance assessment. The score does not certify the correctness or failure of the located solution claim.

cards.title: Log-rank conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Do there exist integers \(C\ge1,k\ge1\) such that every total Boolean function \(f:X\times Y\to\{0,1\}\), for arbitrary nonempty finite sets X and Y, satisfies \(D(f)\le C\bigl(\log_2(r(f)+2)\bigr)^k\)? Here r(f) is the rank over the real numbers of its zero-one communication matrix, and D(f) is its exact deterministic communication complexity in bits.
cards.definitions: Alice receives \(x\in X\), Bob receives \(y\in Y\), and both know the complete function f, its finite domains and their chosen protocol. These shared data are not charged as communication. A protocol is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node specifies its sender and a function from that sender’s input set to \(\{0,1\}\). At that node the sender transmits this one bit, and both parties follow the corresponding edge; the node already records the preceding transcript. Every leaf is labeled 0 or 1. For every pair (x,y), the reached leaf must be labeled f(x,y), so both parties determine the exact answer. The cost is the maximum number of transmitted bits on any input pair, equivalently the tree depth after deleting unreachable branches. D(f) is the minimum cost among all correct trees; a finite protocol always exists. The protocol may depend arbitrarily on f, and its description length, local computation and number of communication rounds have no separate bound or charge. The communication matrix is \(M_f=(f(x,y))_{x\in X,y\in Y}\), treating its zeroes and ones as real scalars. Define \(r(f)=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb R}(M_f)\), the dimension of its column span over \(\mathbb R\). The particular enumeration of either domain does not matter. Rank zero means the all-zero function, which has D(f)=0, and the all-one function also has D(f)=0. The term r+2 avoids a zero or undefined logarithm at small ranks without changing the asymptotic conjecture. The same C and k must work for every choice of domains and function; the protocol need not be generated uniformly from the table. The statement has no promise pairs, missing matrix entries, distribution on inputs, randomness, quantum messages, approximation or one-way restriction. Rank over a finite field, approximate rank and sign rank are not the parameter used here. Some sources encode outputs by minus one and plus one. With \(A=2M_f-J\), where J is the all-one matrix, the two ordinary real ranks differ by at most one and the output relabeling does not change D(f); with the r+2 convention these formulations have the same polynomial-boundedness question. The explicit negation is: for every pair of integers C,k at least one, there exist nonempty finite X,Y and a total f such that \(D(f)>C(\log_2(r(f)+2))^k\). No effective generator of the counterexample functions is added.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a single pair of universal constants C,k satisfying the displayed inequality, or prove its quantified negation excluding every such pair. An affirmative proof must apply to every total function in the exact interactive protocol model; it need not compute an optimal protocol efficiently. A negative proof must give arbitrarily strong failures of polynomial dependence on log-rank, with examples permitted to depend on C and k. Failure of one proposed exponent, a result for partial functions, or a bound using approximate rank, sign rank, randomness or quantum communication does not meet this target.
cards.why: One of the central organizing conjectures of communication complexity. It asks whether a basic linear-algebraic quantity characterizes efficient exact communication, and connects protocols to rectangle partitions, discrepancy, graph structure, and cancellation in matrix decompositions.

importance.reason: A flagship structural conjecture linking deterministic protocols and matrix rank, with many equivalent combinatorial formulations and a large quantitative gap.

progress.text: Lovász and Saks pose the relation between real matrix rank and deterministic communication, as traced in the checked source papers.
Lovett establishes the general upper bound \(O(\sqrt r\log(r+2))\), substantially improving the linear-rank upper bounds.
Göös, Pitassi and Watson prove a nearly quadratic lower bound in log-rank. Their Theorem 2 first concerns one-sided partition number, with the real-rank consequence stated separately.
Sudakov and Tomon obtain \(D(f)=O(\sqrt{r(f)})\). The preprint dates from November 2023, the article appeared online in July 2024, and the journal volume is dated 2025.

Song reports \(\Omega((\log r)^2/\log\log r)\) for an explicit construction. This is a preprint claim with a specific quantitative comparison, not an independently verified catalogue assertion of the strongest bound over all constructions.
The checked third revision of Hambardzumyan–Lovett–Shirley proves the signed-rectangle decomposition theorem and equivalent formulations, and explicitly retains the general conjecture as open.

cards.status_note: The August 2026 equivalent-formulations paper explicitly states that the total deterministic log-rank conjecture remains unresolved, with the square-root-rank upper bound. A bounded primary-source search on 14 September 2026 found no verified resolution. The new lifting proof and its comparison of suppressed logarithmic factors were not independently verified; fixed polynomial lower bounds and partition reformulations do not settle the universal conjecture.

context_blocks.text: Matrix rank gives a general lower bound on communication. A protocol using at most d bits has at most \(2^{d}\) leaves, and the inputs reaching each leaf form a rectangle \(A\times B\). Summing the indicator matrices of the output-one rectangles represents \(M_{f}\) as a sum of at most \(2^{d}\) rank-one matrices. Consequently \(\log _{2}r(f)\le D(f)\) when \(r(f)\ge 1\). The conjecture asks whether this algebraic obstruction controls deterministic communication up to a polynomial.

An elementary upper bound goes in the other direction but is much larger. A rank-r Boolean matrix has at most 2ʳ distinct rows: choose r columns that determine every row, and record their Boolean entries. Alice can identify her row with at most r bits, after which Bob can determine the answer and send one output bit. This protocol makes clear why the question concerns the gap between rank and its logarithm.

A low-rank factorization permits arbitrary real coefficients and cancellation. A protocol instead needs a recursively organized partition into monochromatic rectangles. Moving between these kinds of structure is the main difficulty. Lovett used discrepancy to obtain an \(O(\sqrt{r} \log  r)\) communication bound; Sudakov and Tomon remove the logarithmic factor using a stronger discrepancy estimate for sparse matrices. The resulting \(O(\sqrt{r})\) remains far larger than a polynomial in log r.
Lower-bound constructions show that a linear bound in log-rank is too optimistic. Göös, Pitassi, and Watson obtain a nearly quadratic separation through query-to-communication lifting.

Song’s August 2026 preprint reports an explicit bound \(\Omega((\log r)^2/\log\log r)\) by refining the parameters in earlier constructions. This records the preprint’s stated result, whose proof and comparison of logarithmic losses were not independently verified here. In any event, a lower bound of this fixed polynomial order would not refute the conjecture, which permits a larger universal exponent.

Hambardzumyan, Lovett and Shirley prove that a rank-r Boolean matrix is a signed sum of \(O(r\log(r+2))\) rectangle indicator matrices. Their equivalent conjecture compares this with the minimum number of disjoint all-one rectangles that partition the one-entries. That one-sided partition number differs from both a partition of all entries into monochromatic rectangles and the leaves of a protocol tree. The equivalence is a proved reformulation, not an established bound for exact protocols.

A finite example disproving one proposed constant or exponent would still permit a different polynomial bound. A negative answer must exclude every universal polynomial, with the function and dimensions allowed to vary with that polynomial. A positive answer may choose a different protocol for each function; the conjecture imposes no efficient protocol-construction requirement.

cards.title: Matrix multiplication exponent
cards.formal: Determine, with the absolute \(1/100\) acceptance precision below, the matrix multiplication exponent \(\omega=\inf\{\tau\in\mathbb R:\exists C>0\ \forall n\in\mathbb N,\ n\ge2\Rightarrow s(n)\le Cn^\tau\}\). Here s(n) is the minimum number of arithmetic gates in a circuit computing all entries of the product of two arbitrary n by n complex matrices exactly, in the model below.
cards.definitions: For each integer \(n\ge2\), the inputs are the \(2n^2\) independent complex variables \(a_{ij},b_{ij}\), with \(1\le i,j\le n\). The required n squared outputs are the polynomials \(c_{ij}=\sum_{t=1}^n a_{it}b_{tj}\). A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph whose source nodes are input variables or constants from \(\mathbb C\), and whose other nodes have two ordered inputs and apply addition, subtraction or multiplication. Multiple uses of a previously computed value are allowed. Each ordered output position (i,j) designates a node whose polynomial is exactly c_ij, so one circuit must be correct on every pair of complex matrices. Circuit topology and constants may depend on n, but not on the matrix entries. Size is the number of arithmetic gates, including gates operating on constants; source nodes and output designations have zero cost. No division, comparison, branching, randomness, approximation or test of the input values is permitted. This is a nonuniform algebraic model: a separate finite circuit may be chosen for each n, with no required algorithm generating the circuits or their constants. Scalar arithmetic is exact, and costs of representing complex numbers in bits are outside the model. The number of gates differs only by a constant factor from the source’s binary-circuit wire measure, and allowing an explicit subtraction gate also changes size by at most a constant factor; neither changes the exponent. Define s(n) as the least size among correct circuits. This minimum exists because the elementary multiplication formula gives a circuit, and sizes are nonnegative integers. The n squared output polynomials are distinct and none is a source polynomial, so each needs a distinct arithmetic gate and \(s(n)\ge n^2\). The elementary upper bound \(s(n)\le2n^3\) makes the exponent set nonempty and gives \(2\le\omega\le3\). The infimum need not be attained. Specifically, \(\omega\le u\) means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a real \(C_\varepsilon>0\) such that \(s(n)\le C_\varepsilon n^{u+\varepsilon}\) for every integer n at least two. A lower bound \(\omega\ge\ell\) means that for every real \(\tau<\ell\) and C>0 there is an integer n at least two with \(s(n)>Cn^\tau\). These quantified bounds do not demand a circuit family attaining the endpoint exponent or a pointwise lower bound at that endpoint. The source’s conjecture \(\omega=2\) is one possible value of the numerical target selected for this card.
cards.answer_criterion: Specify a real number a by an unambiguous mathematical description and give a complete Lean-checked proof that \(|a-\omega|\le1/100\) for the unrestricted circuit quantity above. Equivalently, certify bounds \(\ell\le\omega\le u\) with \(u-\ell\le1/50\) and take \(a=(\ell+u)/2\). A proved exact value also qualifies. The proof must justify both sides of the error interval, with the infimum and nonattainment conventions in the definitions. Merely copying or renaming the defining infimum, reporting an optimized upper bound, or giving a bound only for a restricted tensor method does not meet the requirement. This tolerance concerns the value of the exponent and does not assert a proof of the exact conjecture that omega equals two.
cards.why: This exponent measures the asymptotic arithmetic cost of a fundamental operation and governs many other algebraic and graph algorithms. Determining its value would locate the limit of savings from shared computation.

importance.reason: One of the main questions in algebraic algorithms, governing a widely used primitive and many dependent complexity bounds. Both faster constructions and a superquadratic lower bound would have broad consequences.

context_blocks.text: The usual algorithm computes \(n^{2}\) inner products of length n, spending cubic arithmetic work. That computation treats the outputs separately even though they share their input matrices. Strassen’s construction shows that this shared structure can save an asymptotic factor: seven block multiplications replace eight in a two-by-two block product, and recursive use gives exponent \(\log _{2}7\).

The scientific target is the value of the exponent, whether it equals two or is larger. The familiar \(\omega =2\) conjecture specifies one possible answer. Because \(\omega\) is an infimum, an upper bound may approach it with a different circuit family and constant for every positive slack in the exponent. Exact scalar arithmetic over a fixed field separates this quantity from approximate numerical multiplication and hardware throughput.

Modern upper bounds encode multiplication in tensors and exploit savings across large tensor powers. A substantial part of their analysis can be expressed as an optimization over parameters. The August 2026 improvement expands that optimization and uses new search procedures to find better parameters; the paper then describes rational verification of the resulting inequalities. That is an arithmetic exponent result, not an empirical speed comparison.

Alman proves a lower bound of 2.16805 for exponents achievable by applying the universal method to Coppersmith–Winograd tensors. That bound quantifies over a specified tensor framework. It does not imply \(\omega\ge2.16805\), because the quantity in this card permits every arithmetic circuit over the complex numbers.

An improvement in an upper bound and a determination of the exponent are different achievements. Even the reported upper bound 2.371177, together with the elementary lower bound 2, leaves an interval much wider than the required 0.02. A certified value within 0.01 would locate the optimum more closely, while still not necessarily deciding the exact conjecture \(\omega=2\).

cards.title: Hilbert’s tenth problem over the rationals
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine \(A\) that, on every input encoding a polynomial \(f\in\mathbb Z[X_1,\ldots,X_m]\) with \(m\geq1\), halts and outputs YES exactly when \[\exists(q_1,\ldots,q_m)\in\mathbb Q^m\quad f(q_1,\ldots,q_m)=0,\] and outputs NO otherwise? The number of variables, degree and coefficients are unrestricted finite input data, and there is no time or space efficiency requirement.
cards.definitions:
The field \(\mathbb Q\) consists of exact fractions \(a/b\), with \(a\in\mathbb Z\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), identifying fractions of the same value; addition and multiplication are the usual exact field operations. A polynomial input describes \(f=\sum_{j=1}^{r}a_j\prod_{i=1}^{m}X_i^{e_{ji}}\), with \(r\geq0\), \(a_j\in\mathbb Z\) and \(e_{ji}\in\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Repeated monomials and zero coefficients are allowed. The empty sum is the zero polynomial and \(X_i^0=1\), including when evaluating at zero. Constants are represented with all exponents zero. A rational zero is any tuple in \(\mathbb Q^m\) giving exact value zero; there is no bound on its numerators or denominators and no integrality restriction.

Use the following explicit effective binary encoding. For \(u\geq0\), let \(\operatorname{code}(u)=1^b0\operatorname{bin}(u+1)\), where the binary expansion has \(b\) bits and no leading zeroes. Encode an integer \(a\) by a sign bit followed by \(\operatorname{code}(|a|)\), with 0 denoting a nonnegative integer and 1 a negative integer; negative zero is invalid. A complete input is \(\operatorname{code}(m)\operatorname{code}(r)\), followed for each \(j=1,\ldots,r\) by the signed code of \(a_j\) and \(\operatorname{code}(e_{j1}),\ldots,\operatorname{code}(e_{jm})\), with no trailing bits. Require \(m\geq1\). The machine halts and outputs NO on every malformed encoding.

The algorithm is a single finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program with a finite tape alphabet, ordinary discrete transitions and unbounded work tapes, without advice or an oracle. On every input it must halt after finitely many transitions; its running time need not satisfy a polynomial, elementary or other prescribed bound. Its program is independent of \(m,r\), all degrees and all coefficients. The input supplies only the polynomial, without additional height-comparison predicates or a promise of solvability. The question concerns decision of existence; a YES output need not itself contain a rational tuple.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-verified proof of the existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify one effective algorithm and prove termination and exact correctness on every polynomial in the stated domain, together with rejection of invalid input. A negative answer must prove that no such total correct Turing machine exists. Recognizing only polynomials that have a rational zero, excluding polynomial-time algorithms, or proving undecidability for equations with integer-constrained unknowns or added predicates does not establish the required negation. Any conditional result must be identified as conditional and does not alone settle this unconditional question.
cards.why: This asks whether exact rational polynomial constraints admit any general terminating solver. It connects the computability of arithmetic, logical definability and the existence of rational points on algebraic varieties. The unresolved boundary persists despite undecidability over the integers and decidability of polynomial feasibility over the reals and algebraically closed fields; allowing fractions fundamentally changes the permitted witnesses.

importance.reason: A central unsolved decidability problem for an elementary, pervasive constraint language. A resolution would locate the computability boundary for rational polynomial feasibility.

progress.text: The Davis–Putnam–Robinson–Matiyasevich theorem settles the integer-solution problem negatively; rational solvability remains a different decision problem.
Koenigsmann’s Annals paper gives a universal definition of \(\mathbb Z\) in \(\mathbb Q\), implying undecidability of the universal-existential fragment but not the purely existential fragment.
Anscombe and coauthors explicitly record Hilbert’s tenth problem over \(\mathbb Q\) as open and review its relation to existential definability.

The height-comparison undecidability paper appears in Journal of Number Theory after its 2023 preprint. It settles an expansion by height predicates, while retaining the ordinary rational question as open.
The Alpöge–Bhargava–Ho–Shnidman article appears online, proving a negative answer over the ring of integers of every number field; its print issue is March 2026.
Poonen’s account reviews the rings-of-integers breakthrough and gives an alternative proof of the relevant Diophantine-definability implication. Its domain restriction remains essential.

Checked recent results prove undecidability over rings of integers or after adjoining height-comparison predicates; neither settles existence of an unrestricted total rational-solvability decider. This is a formulation and source-scope audit, not an independent verification of every cited proof.

context_blocks.text: Rational tuples can be effectively enumerated and tested by exact substitution, so every YES-instance is eventually recognizable. Such a search does not halt on a NO-instance. The target requires termination in both cases, irrespective of efficiency. A solver for all instances would also allow a rational zero to be found when one exists.

The Davis–Putnam–Robinson–Matiyasevich theorem proves that no general algorithm decides integer solvability. It does not automatically decide the rational problem: \(2X-1=0\) has a rational zero but no integer zero. A rational solver cannot simply be applied to the unchanged integer equation.

Allowing rational coefficients gives the same decision problem, because their denominators can be cleared effectively. Finite systems of equations are also equivalent to a single equation: over \(\mathbb Q\), \(f_1=\cdots=f_r=0\) holds exactly when \(\sum_i f_i^2=0\). More generally, disequalities can be encoded using inverse variables and disjunctions using products. These equivalences identify the problem with decidability of the existential first-order theory of \(\mathbb Q\) in the language of rings.

An existential definition of \(\mathbb Z\) in \(\mathbb Q\) would transfer integer undecidability to this problem. Koenigsmann’s Theorem 1 instead defines \(\mathbb Z\) by a universal formula; its Corollary 3 establishes undecidability for universal-existential sentences. Quantifier alternation is essential to that conclusion: the full first-order theory and the universal-existential fragment are already undecidable, while neither fact settles the purely existential target.

Alpöge, Bhargava, Ho and Shnidman prove undecidability over the ring of integers \(\mathcal O_K\) of every number field \(K\). Here a number field is a finite extension of \(\mathbb Q\), and \(\mathcal O_K\) consists of elements satisfying a monic polynomial with integer coefficients. This restricts the solution domain; in particular \(\mathcal O_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Z\), whereas the present question permits every rational number.

Poonen’s account dated 3 July 2026 reviews the recent proof of undecidability for these rings and supplies an alternative definability argument from rank stability. Its Theorem 4.2 concerns definitions over rings of integers. This account does not extend the negative answer to the whole field \(\mathbb Q\).

Garcia-Fritz, Pasten and Vidaux prove undecidability when rational equations are supplemented with finitely many height-comparison conditions. For a rational tuple \(q\), their logarithmic height is \(h(q)=\log\max\{d,|dq_1|,\ldots,|dq_m|\}\), where \(d\geq1\) is its least common denominator, and the added predicates compare heights of tuples. These extra constraints are absent from the target. Their ordinary rational-solvability question remains explicitly open.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Inactive records are archived outside the catalogue, exports and editorial work. Their content, stable IDs and reasons are retained; imports cannot reactivate them. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Inactive cards, including resolved records, are archived outside the ranking without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
